lessons.title: How IELTS Academic works
lessons.summary: The four papers, their timing, and what each one tests.

steps.title: Four papers, one result
steps.body:
**Listening** — 4 recordings, 40 questions, about 30 minutes. Each recording plays **once**.
**Reading** — 3 passages, 40 questions, **60 minutes**, no extra transfer time.
**Writing** — Task 1 (150+ words, describe a visual) and Task 2 (250+ words, an essay) in **60 minutes**.
**Speaking** — an 11–14 minute interview in three parts.

steps.title: What makes Academic different
steps.body: Reading passages come from books, journals and magazines written for a non-specialist reader. Writing Task 1 always describes data or a diagram — a chart, table, map or process. Listening and Speaking are the same for Academic and General Training.

steps.title: The order of the day
steps.body: Listening, Reading and Writing are taken together without breaks between them. Speaking may be on the same day or up to a week before or after.

steps.question: How many times do you hear each Listening recording?
options: As many times as you like
steps.why: Every recording is played once only, so you must read ahead and predict answers.

steps.question: How long is the Reading paper?
options: 60 minutes plus 10 minutes to transfer answers
steps.why: Academic Reading is 60 minutes with no extra time to transfer answers.

steps.question: Which task always asks you to describe visual information?
steps.why: Academic Task 1 is a report on a chart, table, map or process.

lessons.title: How your band is calculated
lessons.summary: Raw scores, criteria and rounding — so you know where marks come from.

steps.title: Listening and Reading
steps.body: Each is marked out of 40 and converted to a band. Roughly: **30 correct ≈ band 7**, **23 ≈ band 6**, **35 ≈ band 8**. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.

steps.title: Writing and Speaking
steps.body: Each has **four criteria worth 25%**. Writing: Task Achievement/Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Speaking: Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, Pronunciation. **Task 2 counts twice as much as Task 1.**

steps.title: Working out an overall band
steps.body:
Listening 7.0, Reading 6.5, Writing 6.0, Speaking 6.5 → average 6.5 → **overall 6.5**.
If the average ends in .25 it rounds **up** to .5; if it ends in .75 it rounds **up** to the next whole band.

steps.title: Where to win marks
steps.body: Most candidates gain fastest in Listening and Reading (technique) and lose most in Writing (task response and grammar accuracy). Plan your time accordingly.

steps.question: Your bands are L 7, R 7, W 6, S 6.5. The average is 6.625. What is your overall band?
steps.why: 6.625 is nearer 6.5 than 7.0; only .25 and .75 averages round up.

steps.question: Which writing task carries more weight?
steps.why: Task 2 is worth twice as much as Task 1.

lessons.title: A study routine that works
lessons.summary: How to practise so that your band actually moves.

steps.title: Little and often
steps.body: 30–45 minutes every day beats one long session a week. Spread practice across all four skills, and spend extra time on your weakest one.

steps.title: Keep an error log
steps.body: After every practice, copy each mistake into a list: the wrong version, the right version and the reason. Review the list daily. The Corrections section of each writing report gives you these directly.

steps.title: Review vocabulary with spaced repetition
steps.body: The Vocabulary module brings back each word just before you forget it. Ten minutes a day of reviews is enough to remember hundreds of words.

steps.question: Which plan is likely to improve your band most?
options: 40 minutes every day, rotating skills, plus a weekly mock
steps.answer: 40 minutes every day, rotating skills, plus a weekly mock
steps.why: Regular, varied practice with feedback works better than occasional long sessions.

lessons.title: Read ahead and predict
lessons.summary: Use the reading time to know what you are listening for.

steps.title: Before the audio starts
steps.body: You get time to read each set of questions. Use it to underline key words and **predict the type of answer**: a number, a date, a name, a noun, an adjective.

steps.title: Predicting
steps.body:
Question: *Course starts: ______ March*
Prediction: a **date or ordinal number** (e.g. 9th).
Question: *Students must bring an ______*
Prediction: a **singular noun beginning with a vowel sound** (because of 'an').

steps.title: Follow the order
steps.body: Answers come in the same order as the questions. If you miss one, move on — don't lose the next three looking for it.

steps.question: 'The tour costs £______ per person.' What should you listen for?
steps.why: The £ sign tells you the answer is an amount of money.

steps.question: You missed question 4 and the speaker is now clearly talking about question 6. What should you do?
options: Guess question 4 later and focus on 6
steps.answer: Guess question 4 later and focus on 6
steps.why: Answers come in order, so question 4 has passed. Guess it at the end.

lessons.title: Form and note completion
lessons.summary: Spelling, numbers and word limits — easy marks that are easy to lose.

steps.title: Check the word limit
steps.body: 'ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER' means *one word*, *one number*, or *one word and one number* — never two words. A wrong word count makes the answer wrong even if the meaning is right.

steps.title: Spelling counts
steps.body: Names are often spelled letter by letter. Practise the alphabet sounds that are easy to confuse: **A/E/I**, **G/J**, **B/V**, **M/N**. Plurals matter too: 'apron' and 'aprons' are different answers.

steps.title: Numbers and dates
steps.body:
'thirteen' vs 'thirty' — listen to the stress: thir**TEEN** vs **THIR**ty.
Dates can be written 9 March, 9th March or March 9 — all accepted.

steps.question: Instruction: ONE WORD ONLY. You hear 'a large leather bag'. Which answer is acceptable for 'a large ______'?
steps.why: Only one word is allowed, and 'large' is already printed.

steps.question: Which pair is most often confused in spelling tasks?
steps.why: G /dʒiː/ and J /dʒeɪ/ sound similar to many learners.

lessons.title: Distractors and corrections
lessons.summary: Speakers change their minds. The first thing you hear is often wrong.

steps.title: How distractors work
steps.body: The recording often mentions **two or three possible answers**, then rejects all but one. Listen for signals: *actually*, *sorry, I mean*, *no, that's changed*, *it used to be*, *but*.

steps.title: Spot the change
steps.body:
*'It was going to start on the second, but the studio is being repainted, so we moved it back to the ninth.'*
Answer: **9th** — not the 2nd.

steps.question: 'The meeting is on Tuesday — oh no, wait, it was moved to Thursday this week.' When is the meeting?
steps.why: 'Oh no, wait' signals a correction; the final information is the answer.

steps.question: 'The full price is £120, but members pay £95.' The question asks for the member price.
steps.why: The question is about members; £120 is the distractor.

lessons.title: Maps and plans
lessons.summary: The direction language you need to follow a tour.

steps.title: Orient yourself first
steps.body: Find the starting point ('You are here', the entrance) and the compass if there is one. Then follow the speaker's route with your pencil.

steps.title: Key language
steps.body: **opposite**, **next to / beside**, **in the corner**, **at the far end**, **to the left of**, **straight ahead**, **go past**, **turn right**, **just before you reach**, **north / south-east of**.

steps.question: 'Go past the café and the toilets are on your right, just before the exit.' Where are the toilets?
options: Between the café and the exit
steps.answer: Between the café and the exit
steps.why: You pass the café first and find the toilets before you reach the exit.

lessons.title: Skimming and scanning
lessons.summary: Two reading speeds and when to use each.

steps.title: Skim for the shape
steps.body: Spend **1–2 minutes** reading the title, the first sentence of each paragraph and any names or numbers. Note in a few words what each paragraph is about.

steps.title: Scan for the answer
steps.body: For each question, pick a **search word** that is easy to spot — a name, a date, a number, a technical term — and run your eyes down the text to find it. Then read that part slowly.

steps.title: Paraphrase is the rule
steps.body: Questions rarely use the passage's words. Expect *'not enough money'* to appear as *'insufficient funding'*. Every reading test in this app shows you the paraphrase pairs after you submit.

steps.question: Which is the best word to scan for in: 'In 1873, Harrison's watch was tested on a voyage to Jamaica'?
steps.why: Numbers and names stand out on the page and are rarely paraphrased.

steps.question: Passage: 'funding was insufficient'. Which question wording is a paraphrase?
steps.why: Same meaning, different words — exactly how IELTS questions are written.

lessons.title: True / False / Not Given
lessons.summary: The question type most candidates get wrong — and how to stop.

steps.title: The three answers
steps.body:
**TRUE / YES** — the passage says the same thing.
**FALSE / NO** — the passage says the opposite, or something that cannot be true at the same time.
**NOT GIVEN** — the passage does not say; you would need outside knowledge to decide.

steps.title: Facts vs opinions
steps.body: True/False/Not Given checks **facts** in the passage. Yes/No/Not Given checks the **writer's views or claims**. The method is the same.

steps.title: Watch the qualifiers
steps.body: Words like **all, most, some, only, always, never, first, mainly** are the usual trap. 'Most species' in the passage and 'All species' in the statement → FALSE.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Passage: *'Street trees typically survive for only a fraction of the lifespan they would reach in woodland.'*
1. 'Street trees live shorter lives than woodland trees.' → **TRUE**
2. 'Street trees grow faster in their first years.' → **NOT GIVEN** (growth rate is never mentioned)
3. 'Street trees live longer than woodland trees.' → **FALSE**

steps.question: Passage: 'Most of the microorganisms had never been described.' Statement: 'Scientists already knew all of the microorganisms.'
steps.why: The passage says most were unknown, which contradicts 'knew all'.

steps.question: Passage: 'The museum opened in 1998 with 200 paintings.' Statement: 'The museum was popular with tourists.'
steps.why: Nothing is said about tourists or popularity.

steps.question: Passage: 'Only a few cities have laws protecting soil.' Statement: 'Few cities legally protect soil.'
steps.why: 'Only a few cities have laws' paraphrases 'few cities legally protect'.

lessons.title: Matching headings
lessons.summary: Find the main idea, not a matching word.

steps.title: Main idea first
steps.body: Read the paragraph and decide its **main idea** before you look at the headings. The main idea is usually in the first or last sentence, but check the whole paragraph.

steps.title: Beware the word match
steps.body: Wrong headings often repeat a word from a **detail** in the paragraph. A heading must describe the whole paragraph, not one sentence of it.

steps.title: Use elimination
steps.body: Do the paragraphs you are sure about first and cross out their headings. There are always more headings than paragraphs.

steps.question: A paragraph describes three studies, all showing that noise harms sleep, and mentions 'traffic' once. Best heading?
steps.why: It covers the whole paragraph; 'traffic' is only a detail.

lessons.title: Matching features and information
lessons.summary: Linking statements to people, places or paragraphs.

steps.title: Matching features
steps.body: You match statements to a list (researchers, countries, dates). **Scan for each name** in the passage and underline it — names are easy to find. Then compare what is said near each name with the statements. Letters may be used more than once.

steps.title: Matching information
steps.body: You find which **paragraph** contains a piece of information (an example, a reason, a comparison). These are **not in passage order**, so do them after the questions that are.

steps.question: In a matching-features task the instructions say 'You may use any letter more than once'. What does this tell you?
options: Each person matches exactly one statement
One person may match several statements
steps.answer: One person may match several statements
steps.why: So do not cross out a letter after using it.

lessons.title: Summary and sentence completion
lessons.summary: Grammar is your best clue to the missing word.

steps.title: Read around the gap
steps.body: Decide what kind of word fits: **noun, verb, adjective, number**. Check singular/plural and articles: *'an ______'* needs a word starting with a vowel sound.

steps.title: Word bank or passage?
steps.body: If there is a **box of options**, the answer is a letter and the words will be paraphrased. If there is no box, **copy the words exactly** from the passage, within the word limit.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Summary: *'Lamps can be fitted with ______ so that light does not escape upwards.'*
A noun is needed (after 'with'). The passage says *'fully shielded fixtures direct all light downward'* → **shields**.

steps.question: 'The researchers found that the plants needed more ______ to grow.' Which word type fits?
steps.why: 'more ______' followed by 'to grow' needs an uncountable noun.

lessons.title: Multiple choice
lessons.summary: Every option is in the text somewhere — only one answers the question.

steps.title: Question first
steps.body: Read the **question stem** carefully and find the right place in the passage before reading the options. Then check each option against that part of the text.

steps.title: Why wrong options look right
steps.body: Distractors use words from the passage but change the meaning: the wrong cause, a different time, someone else's opinion, or a claim that goes too far. After each reading test, the app explains why each wrong option is wrong.

steps.question: The passage says a method 'may help some patients'. Which option is most likely a distractor?
options: The method is useful for certain patients.
The method could benefit some people.
steps.why: It goes too far: 'cures all' is much stronger than 'may help some'.

lessons.title: Managing 60 minutes
lessons.summary: A timing plan for three passages.

steps.title: A simple plan
steps.body: Passage 1: **17 minutes**. Passage 2: **20 minutes**. Passage 3: **23 minutes**. Passage 3 is the hardest, so protect its time.

steps.title: Never get stuck
steps.body: If a question takes more than 90 seconds, guess and mark it. Come back at the end if there is time. An unanswered question is always wrong; a guess sometimes isn't.

steps.question: You have 5 minutes left and 4 questions unanswered. What should you do?
steps.why: There is no penalty for wrong answers.

lessons.title: Task 1: the overview
lessons.summary: The single most important sentence in your report.

steps.title: What an overview is
steps.body: An overview describes the **two or three biggest features** of the visual — the main trends, the largest and smallest, the clearest contrast — **without detailed figures**. Start it with *'Overall,'*.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Without a clear overview, Task Achievement **cannot go above band 5**, however good your language is.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: *'Overall, internet access rose sharply in all four regions, and by 2025 almost every household had a connection. The West led throughout, while the South started furthest behind.'*

steps.title: A reliable structure
steps.body:
1. Introduction: paraphrase the question in one sentence.
2. Overview: the main features.
3. Body 1: one group of details with figures.
4. Body 2: the other group, with comparisons.

steps.question: Which sentence is an overview?
options: In 2005, 32% of households in the North had internet.
Overall, access grew everywhere, with the West always highest.
I think the internet is very important.
steps.answer: Overall, access grew everywhere, with the West always highest.
steps.why: It summarises the main trend and the main comparison without detailed figures.

steps.question: Should you explain why the numbers changed?
options: No, only describe what the data shows
steps.answer: No, only describe what the data shows
steps.why: Reasons and opinions are not in the data and lower your Task Achievement band.

lessons.title: Task 1: describing change and comparison
lessons.summary: The verbs, nouns and adverbs examiners expect.

steps.title: Change
steps.body:
**Up:** rise, increase, grow, climb, surge
**Down:** fall, decrease, decline, drop, plunge
**Flat:** remain stable, level off, plateau
**Degree:** sharply, dramatically, significantly, steadily, gradually, slightly

steps.title: Two patterns
steps.body:
Verb + adverb: *'Sales **rose sharply**.'*
Adjective + noun: *'There was **a sharp rise** in sales.'*
Using both patterns shows grammatical range.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body: *twice as many as*, *a third of*, *considerably higher than*, *the largest proportion*, *whereas*, *while*, *in contrast*.

steps.question: Choose the accurate sentence.
options: The number of cars increased sharply.
The number of cars were increasing sharp.
There was a sharply increase of cars.
steps.answer: The number of cars increased sharply.
steps.why: 'The number' is singular, and an adverb (sharply) describes a verb.

steps.question: Values went from 210 to 150. Which description fits?
steps.why: A drop of 60 from 210 is a large decrease.

lessons.title: Task 1: maps and processes
lessons.summary: Different visuals, different language.

steps.title: Maps
steps.body: Compare **before and after**. Use the passive: *'A car park **was built** to the north of the station. The trees **were cut down** to make way for housing.'* Mention what stayed the same too.

steps.title: Processes
steps.body: Count the stages and describe them **in order** with sequencers: *first, next, after that, once…, finally*. Use the present simple passive: *'The leaves **are dried** and then **ground** into powder.'*

steps.question: Which tense is usually right for a manufacturing process?
steps.why: Processes describe general facts; the passive focuses on what happens, not who does it.

lessons.title: Task 2: understanding the question
lessons.summary: Answer every part, or Task Response stops at 5.

steps.title: Five common types
steps.body:
**Opinion** — To what extent do you agree?
**Discussion** — Discuss both views and give your opinion.
**Advantages/disadvantages** — Do the advantages outweigh…?
**Problem/solution** — What problems… what can be done?
**Two-part** — two direct questions to answer.

steps.title: Underline every part
steps.body: Find the **topic**, the **specific angle** and every **instruction**. 'Discuss both views **and give your opinion**' has three jobs: view one, view two, your view.

steps.title: Example
steps.body:
*'Some people think universities should only offer subjects useful for employment. Others think students should study what interests them. **Discuss both views and give your opinion.**'*
Jobs: (1) the employment view, (2) the interest view, (3) your position — stated in the introduction and the conclusion.

steps.question: 'What are the causes of obesity, and what can governments do about it?' How many parts must you answer?
steps.why: Causes, and government action. Missing either limits Task Response.

lessons.title: Task 2: a structure that scores
lessons.summary: Four paragraphs, 270–300 words.

steps.title: The plan
steps.body:
1. **Introduction** (2 sentences): paraphrase the question and give your position.
2. **Body 1**: one main idea, explained and supported.
3. **Body 2**: a second main idea.
4. **Conclusion** (1–2 sentences): answer the question again in new words.

steps.title: Developing a paragraph
steps.body:
**P**oint — the topic sentence.
**E**xplain — why or how.
**E**xample — specific and realistic.
**L**ink — back to the question.
Two developed ideas beat four listed ones.

steps.title: A developed body paragraph
steps.body: *'The main argument for career-focused degrees is financial. Students often borrow heavily to study, so they need qualifications that lead to secure jobs. In the UK, for instance, graduates in engineering earn far more on average than those in many arts subjects. For many families, therefore, employability is a sensible priority.'*

steps.question: What is the biggest weakness of a body paragraph that lists four reasons in four sentences?
steps.why: Band 7 Task Response needs main ideas that are extended and supported.

lessons.title: Cohesion without the clichés
lessons.summary: Linking words help — until you overuse them.

steps.title: Mechanical linking caps your band
steps.body: Starting every sentence with *Moreover*, *Furthermore*, *In addition* is a band 6 feature: cohesion is 'mechanical'. Band 7 uses **a range of devices flexibly**.

steps.title: Use reference words
steps.body: Link ideas with **this, these, such, it, they, the former, the latter**, and by repeating ideas with synonyms: *'Governments should tax sugary drinks. **This measure** would…'*

steps.question: Which link is most natural?
options: This policy is also inexpensive to introduce.
steps.answer: This policy is also inexpensive to introduce.
steps.why: Reference ('This policy') plus 'also' links smoothly without a heavy connector.

lessons.title: Grammar errors that cost bands
lessons.summary: The mistakes examiners see most — and the fixes.

steps.title: Agreement
steps.body:
*The number of students **is** rising.* (the number = singular)
*People **are** …* (people = plural)
*Everyone **has** …* (everyone = singular)

steps.title: Countable or not
steps.body: **information, advice, research, equipment, knowledge** have no plural: *much information*, *a piece of advice*, *some research*.

steps.title: Articles
steps.body: Use **the** for something specific or unique (*the government*, *the environment*). No article for general plurals and uncountables: *Children need exercise.*

steps.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: There is a lot of information online.
steps.answer: There is a lot of information online.
steps.why: 'Information' is uncountable.

steps.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The number of tourists have increased.
The number of tourists has increased.
A number of tourist has increased.
steps.answer: The number of tourists has increased.
steps.why: 'The number' takes a singular verb.

steps.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Pollution is serious problem in the cities.
Pollution is a serious problem in cities.
The pollution is the serious problem in the cities.
steps.answer: Pollution is a serious problem in cities.
steps.why: 'A' for a singular countable noun; no article for general plurals.

lessons.title: Part 1: extend your answers
lessons.summary: Answer, reason, detail — in two or three sentences.

steps.title: Not too short, not a speech
steps.body: A one-word answer shows nothing. A two-minute answer wastes the examiner's time. Aim for **2–3 sentences**: answer → reason → example or detail.

steps.title: Weak vs strong
steps.body:
Q: *Do you like reading?*
Weak: *'Yes, I do.'*
Strong: *'Yes, quite a lot — mostly novels. I find it's the best way to switch off after a busy day, and I usually read for half an hour before bed.'*

steps.question: Which answer is best for 'Do you work or study?'
options: I'm studying civil engineering in my second year. It's demanding, but I enjoy the practical projects.
I am a student and I study and my subject is engineering and I like it and…
steps.answer: I'm studying civil engineering in my second year. It's demanding, but I enjoy the practical projects.
steps.why: A direct answer, a detail and a reason, in natural sentences.

lessons.title: Part 2: the long turn
lessons.summary: Use the minute well and keep talking for two.

steps.title: The preparation minute
steps.body: Write **2–3 key words per bullet**, not sentences. Decide your story quickly — a true story is easiest, but an invented one is fine; you are marked on language, not truth.

steps.title: Fill two minutes
steps.body: Cover every bullet, and spend the most time on the **'and explain…'** bullet — that is where your range shows. Add feelings, a short anecdote, and what you would do differently.

steps.title: If you run out
steps.body: Go back to a bullet and add an example, or compare the past and the present. Keep going until the examiner stops you.

steps.question: What should your notes look like?
options: A few key words per bullet
steps.answer: A few key words per bullet
steps.why: Key words are fast to write and stop you reading aloud.

lessons.title: Part 3: discussing ideas
lessons.summary: Move from personal to general and give balanced opinions.

steps.title: Think bigger
steps.body: Part 3 questions are about **society**, not you. Talk about people, governments, generations, the future. Give an opinion, explain it, give an example, and consider another view.

steps.title: Useful language
steps.body: *It depends on…* · *On the one hand… on the other…* · *I'd argue that…* · *A good example of this is…* · *In the future, I expect…* · *That's a difficult question, but…*

steps.question: Q: 'Should governments pay for university education?' Which start is most Part 3-like?
options: I went to university last year.
I'd argue that they should, at least partly, because an educated workforce benefits everyone.
steps.answer: I'd argue that they should, at least partly, because an educated workforce benefits everyone.
steps.why: A clear position with a general reason, ready to be extended with an example.

lessons.title: Fluency and pronunciation
lessons.summary: What the examiner actually listens for.

steps.title: Fluency is not speed
steps.body: Fluency means speaking at length **without long pauses** and linking ideas naturally. Use thinking phrases instead of silence: *'That's an interesting question, let me think…'*

steps.title: Pronunciation is being easy to understand
steps.body: You do not need a British or American accent. Focus on **word stress** (de**VEL**op, e**CON**omy), **sentence stress** on key words, and clear final consonants (*worked*, *tests*).

steps.title: Practise with the app
steps.body: In each speaking test, the report shows your words per minute and long pauses. Aim for 120+ words per minute with few pauses over a second.

steps.question: Where is the stress in 'economy'?
steps.why: /ɪˈkɒnəmi/ — the second syllable is stressed.
